1:
Who stands on the sand is disputed first. John Gill reports that the Latin, Syriac and Ethiopic versions and the Alexandrian copy read “he stood,” meaning the dragon left raging at the close of the preceding chapter, and thinks that the better reading, since the connection requires it and there is no mention here of John being called or removed. Charles Ellicott agrees and would translate it so, noting that some editors make the clause a separate verse closing the previous chapter; the dragon stands on the shore and summons his legions like the superior fiend of the English poet, and two monsters rise at his bidding, one of more brutal and the other of more subtle power. A.T. Robertson takes the same subject from the passive verb, rendering that the dragon stopped on his way to war with the rest of the woman’s seed, though he records manuscripts reading “I stood.” Against these, Matthew Henry keeps the seer as subject, standing as it seemed to himself on the sea-shore though probably still in a rapture, and John Wesley says only that this too was in the vision.

What the sea and the beast signify is answered from Daniel. Charles Ellicott makes the sea the restless mass of humankind, swayed by impulse as waves make up an ocean, and observes that the word chosen implies the predominance of the beast nature: whatever power rises here rules not by love or right but by fear and wilfulness. A.T. Robertson traces the imagery to Daniel 7:3 and calls it a vast empire used in the interest of brute force, noting that here the horns are crowned, not the heads. Bede reads the sea as the abyss and the beast as the body of the devil, springing from the people of the ungodly. Adam Clarke insists on method first: the symbol must be fixed from Scripture, since the Holy Ghost is his own interpreter and what a term means in one prophetic vision it must mean in another; and the angel’s explanation of Daniel’s fourth beast, that it is a fourth kingdom upon earth, settles what a beast is.

Which power is meant divides them. A.T. Robertson names the Roman Empire, supporting it from the blasphemous titles the emperors took, attested by inscriptions where the word for god is constantly applied to them. Albert Barnes narrows it to the secular Roman power that upheld the church of Rome through all its corrupt and bloody progress, and calls the beast’s derivation of power and seat from the dragon a striking figure of Satan’s power put forth on earth. John Wesley identifies it with the Roman papacy as it stood in his own day, a spiritually secular power opposed to the kingdom of Christ, neither merely ecclesiastical nor merely political but a mixture, since a crown and a kingdom are ascribed to it while it is also a false prophet; and he warns that the subject is no point of curiosity but a solemn warning. Victorinus of Pettau refers it to the kingdom of the time of Antichrist and the people mingled out of many nations.

The composite animal is read part by part. Bede assigns the leopard to the diversity of the nations, the bear to malice and fury, the lion to strength of body and pride of tongue, and recalls that Daniel compared the Chaldeans to a lioness, the Persians to a bear, the Macedonians to a leopard. Victorinus of Pettau takes the bear’s feet for its leaders and the lion’s mouth for a mouth armed for blood, whose bidding is its weapon. Matthew Henry sums it as a composition of the three, with the fierceness and strength and swiftness of them all, and assigns the seven heads to its several powers, the ten crowns to its tributary princes, and the name of blasphemy to its open enmity against the glory of God.
2:
Why the beast is composite is answered from Daniel in four ways. Albert Barnes observes that John has combined into one monster all the animals Daniel brought successively on the scene — the lion for the Babylonian power, the bear for the Medo-Persian, the leopard for the Macedonian, and a nondescript for the Roman — and finds a propriety in it, since the Roman power was made up of the empires the earlier symbols stood for. A.T. Robertson agrees that the strength and brutality of the Babylonian, Median and Persian empires reappeared in the Roman, and adds that the leopard was reckoned a cross between a panther and a lioness. Charles Ellicott takes the combination as representative rather than historical, since the beast stands for every form of world-power swift to shed blood — leaping on the prey like a leopard, tenacious and relentless as a bear, all-devouring as a lion — and compares the three beasts that hindered the poet from ascending the pleasant mount — luxuriousness, cruel ambition, heartless avarice. Adam Clarke presses the leopard alone, as an allusion to Daniel’s third beast and so to the Greek empire, and works out a resemblance between that empire and the Latin: both held an idolatrous system professedly Christian but really antichristian, and in both the civil authority was depressed by the ecclesiastical.

On the grant of power they agree. Charles Ellicott would render the second gift as his throne rather than his seat, and observes that it is through this succession of world-powers that the dragon carries on his war, the beast becoming his vicegerent. A.T. Robertson puts it more shortly: the beast is Satan’s agent, and Satan claimed this very power when he offered it to Christ in the wilderness.

The wounded head is the hardest question in the chapter, and Albert Barnes says so outright, calling it among the most perplexing inquiries in the whole book. He defines the wound as one which would naturally have been fatal had something not prevented the result, and notes that John says neither who inflicted it nor what it was; and he notes that the heads are said elsewhere to be both seven mountains and seven kings, fixing the location on the seven hills and suggesting a succession of administrations. John Gill takes the head to be the sixth form of government, that of the emperors, and refers the stroke to the destruction of Rome itself, the city built on seven mountains. Adam Clarke agrees that the heads must be forms of government and identifies the wounded one with the imperial power, wounded to death when the northern nations overturned the empire and the very name of emperor ended in the last of the western line; the wound looked past healing, since the west fell to several barbarous nations, and yet it was healed when a new line assumed all the marks and titles of the ancient emperors.

Two of them refuse that reading entirely. A.T. Robertson notes that the participle is the very one used of the slain Lamb, and refers the death-stroke to the suicide of Nero, after which pretenders arose claiming to be Nero as late as twenty years on, so that John seems to regard Domitian as Nero over again; the distinction between the beast and its heads is not always preserved. Charles Ellicott takes the same word about the Lamb in the opposite direction: the death-blow is the one just dealt, when the seed of the woman bruised the serpent’s head, and the stroke that cast down the dragon fell on his agent too, since in overthrowing the wicked one Christ struck at every system founded on passion, self-sufficiency or inhumanity. That the wound is apparently healed then tells the Church that the fruits of the victory will not be seen without delay, and that evil rises again with new vigour contrary to all expectation.
4:
What the worship of verse 4 amounts to divides them. Albert Barnes defines the verb narrowly: it means properly to kiss, or to kiss one’s own hand and extend it towards a person in token of respect, and it is not always used in a religious sense, being paid to kings and princes and to parents as well as to God; so he takes the homage here as reverence rendered to a higher power rather than open adoration of the dragon as God, while asking whether the power set up under Papal Rome, civil and ecclesiastical, was not such as Satan approved, and whether homage so contrary to the law of God was not in fact paid to the presiding spirit of evil. A.T. Robertson allows no such softening: they really worshipped Satan when they worshipped the beast or any one of its heads, the beast being merely the tool of the devil for worship, and emperor-worship, like all idolatry, was devil-worship — the devil having once proposed that Jesus worship him. Adam Clarke reads it institutionally, as the voluntary religious subjection of the members of the Latin Church to the revived western empire because of the part it took in supporting their faith. John Gill locates it in the objects: the devil is worshipped in the idols, images, angels and departed saints to whom adoration is given, as the Gentiles did, whose successors they are and whose name they bear.

The two acclamations are heard as parody and as boast. A.T. Robertson catches in the first an echo, perhaps a parody, of language used of God in the song at the sea and in the Psalms, and observes that the second justifies worship purely on the ground of brute force — the doctrine that might makes right, which he then turns on his own century as self-worship under a new name. Adam Clarke supplies the documentary counterpart, that most invincible was the peculiar attribute of the emperors of Germany, and paraphrases the boast as a claim to be the only holy power in the universe, outside which none can be saved.

On the mouth given him, Albert Barnes notes that John does not say by whom it was given, and infers the dragon of the previous verse; the language is that used of the little horn in Daniel, and the claims are of divine right, of power over liberty, property and conscience, and of the right to give absolute law. John Gill insists the permission is double: the beast was stirred up by the dragon, yet the speaking was given him, so that his coming was after the working of Satan but not without the will of God. Charles Ellicott draws consolation from the same passive, that he has no power beyond what is given, and that behind the reckless and apparently irresistible power there stands the veiled but real power of God.

The forty-two months are read three ways. Adam Clarke and Albert Barnes both take them as prophetic, a day for a year, so twelve hundred and sixty years; Clarke adds that the terminus cannot at present be ascertained, since the beginning is not indubitably known. Charles Ellicott is content to call it the familiar period, the limited time of the world-power. A.T. Robertson stays with the grammar, weighing whether the verb means working signs for that duration or simply doing time, as a man does his hours in the vineyard. On the object of the blasphemy, Ellicott would translate them that tabernacle in the heaven, since much of the beauty is lost by dwell: the saints may tabernacle their spirits where their treasure is even now. Barnes takes the tabernacle for the true church, God’s dwelling-place on earth, and finds the fulfilment in the anathemas and excommunications pronounced through the long period of Papal rule.
7:
That the beast makes war with the saints and overcomes them is read by four of them as history and by one as something short of it. John Gill takes the war both spiritually and literally — not merely anathemas, excommunications and bulls, but the temporal sword, pitched battles and armies — and thinks a special regard may be had to the war on the Waldenses and Albigenses, in which he reports a million slain, together with the bloody Inquisition, murders and massacres. Albert Barnes reads the same fulfilment and grounds the wording on Daniel, where the same horn made war with the saints and prevailed against them; the claim to universal dominion, with the right of deposing kings and giving away kingdoms, answers to the power given over every kindred and tongue. Adam Clarke piles up the arithmetic he has from an older writer — a million in France alone, nine hundred thousand in little more than thirty years from the founding of the Jesuits, a hundred and fifty thousand destroyed by the Inquisition — and adds the point his source concedes, that many were put to death not by pope and bishops but by the civil magistrates, which is precisely his dragon in a new shape.

Charles Ellicott will not let conquest mean what it seems to mean. He would translate the verbs as present, he makes war and conquers them, and then defines the conquest down: it is not a conquest of their fidelity, only that the beast so far succeeds that they must suffer or submit. The saints seem to be single handed, since authority is given him over every tribe and people; and the next verse shows how completely the earth is at his feet. A.T. Robertson keeps to the text and its manuscripts, noting that the whole clause about the war is absent from several witnesses, probably lost by like ending after the repeated it was given; the words themselves come from Daniel, and the sense is plain enough — there was no escape from the beast’s rule in the Mediterranean world.

The universality of the worship in verse 8 raises the question of who is exempted, and the answer is the same in all of them: those whose names stand in the Lamb’s book. Albert Barnes pictures a register kept by the Lord Jesus in which the names of all who shall obtain everlasting life are recorded. Charles Ellicott makes the exemption the point of the whole verse — the saints, though conquered, conquer, since they do not worship after the fashion of the deluded or the self-seeking, a stronger tie binding them to a better allegiance, and their security rests on the eternal love of God, an eternal deliverer being the only refuge from so great a world-tyranny. A.T. Robertson notices that the relative is singular where the antecedent is plural, which throws the responsibility for emperor-worship on the individual, and that the perfect tense means the name stands written, a permanent state.

Where the phrase from the foundation of the world belongs is left open by most of them. Albert Barnes reports the alternative construction, that the names were not written from the foundation of the world, and allows that either makes good sense, but keeps the common version as the simplest; he is careful to add that the Lamb was not actually put to death then, only that the intention was formed then and so constantly represented by bloody sacrifices that it might be spoken of as done. A.T. Robertson weighs the same two attachments, finds the most natural use with slain, and rests on the death of Christ lying in the purpose of God. John Gill is content to identify the worshippers as men who are of the earth, earthly, seeking only earthly honours, pleasures and profits.
9:
The call to hear is taken by all of them as a marker of weight rather than as new matter. John Gill says the mystical description of antichrist is both difficult and of great moment, and is to be considered seriously so that a man may know him and his followers and avoid them. Albert Barnes makes it simply a notice that what has been said of the beast is worthy of special attention, pertaining as it does to the most important events in the history of the church. Adam Clarke divides the function in two: the words impress the reader with the awfulness of what has just been spoken and fix his attention on what follows. Charles Ellicott hears an echo of his Master’s words on the lips of the beloved disciple, calling marked attention to the warning of the next verse. A.T. Robertson notes only that it is a condition of the first class and a repetition of the saying sent to each of the seven churches.

Verse 10 they read in opposite directions. Albert Barnes takes the Greek as deliberately general — if any one leadeth into captivity — and draws a general truth from it: men and nations are dealt with according to their character and their treatment of others, so that nations characterised by war and conquest may expect the lot they have brought on others, which he matches with the Saviour’s word that all they that take the sword shall perish with the sword. He then applies it particularly — invading countries, enslaving peoples, setting up unjust dominion, imprisoning the innocent — and calls it strikingly descriptive of Rome under the republic or the empire, secular or ecclesiastical, Pagan or Papal. Adam Clarke reads it the same way and presses the reason: the Latin empire must go into captivity because it led others into captivity, compelling nations to embrace its system under penalty of forfeiting the empire’s protection, and must be broken by the sword because it killed the saints of God; but the full accomplishment waits until the kingdoms of this world become Christ’s. John Gill puts devil and antichrist together as the captors who shall themselves be taken and cast into the lake that burns with fire and brimstone.

Charles Ellicott reports the general understanding — a caution to the suffering saints that there is nothing for them but to endure, as Jeremiah told his countrymen that those for death must go out to meet it — and then asks whether it is not something else: a warning that the way of the Church’s victory lay through suffering captivity and meeting the sword, and that the temptation to seize the weapons of their foes would be fatal to their true success. Their weapons are those of faith and patience, truth and righteousness, and they must accept the tribulation as their Lord accepted His cross — which is itself the witness that the sword will turn against those who use it. A.T. Robertson arrives at the same counsel by grammar, taking the first clause as a warning to Christians not to resist force with force but to accept captivity as a means of grace, as John himself had done, while cautioning that the text is not certain; the second he reads as a picture of the persecutor, with the inevitable conclusion that the killer is killed.

What the closing words commend follows from each reading. Clarke has God calling His saints to keep His retributive justice in view under all their persecutions, no violence having been done them that shall not be retaliated on their persecutors. Ellicott locates the endurance precisely in not seizing easy, world-like methods of saving themselves. Robertson observes that the faith named here is more like faithfulness or fidelity, and that the here means this attitude of submission to the inevitable.
11:
What the second beast is divides them, and the majority reading is ecclesiastical. John Gill says it is the same beast in substance though not in show: the first is the pope at the head of the ten kingdoms, in his secular character; this is the same pope with his clergy, now a spiritual lord, pretending great humility and holiness while obliging men to idolatry. Matthew Henry sets out the two constructions in play — those who make the first beast pagan Rome take the second for papal Rome, promoting the same idolatry in a softer and more lamb-like manner, while those who make the first the secular power of the papacy take the second for its spiritual powers, acting under the disguise of religion and charity to souls — and he settles on the latter, rejecting an older identification of the impostor with a pagan wonder-worker. The pope shows the horns of a lamb, pretending to be the vicar of Christ, but his speech betrays him: the false doctrines and cruel decrees he gives forth show him to belong to the dragon and not to the Lamb.

Albert Barnes builds the same identification out of the two elements. The first rose from the sea, a power born of a perturbed state of affairs, as the secular power that sustained the Papacy rose out of the invasions of the northern hordes and the convulsions of the falling empire; this rises from the land, firmer than the waters, because the spiritual power grew up under a more settled order and was comparatively calm in its origin. The lamb-like horns he calls a most striking representation of the way that power has always been put forth, laying claim to great meekness. Adam Clarke reads the same figure as chronology: earth means the Latin world, so the beast springs from a state of subjection within it, and he dates the emergence: the ecclesiastical power was subject to the civil in the time of Charlemagne and long after, gained ground through the tenth century, rose above the emperors themselves, and was at length entirely exempted from the civil power, so constituting another beast.

Charles Ellicott declines historical identification. Both wild beasts rise from beneath; the sea is the tumultuous passions of mankind, the earth the more fixed element of human thought and wisdom, society consolidated by intelligence and culture — but the wisdom guiding this one is what a sacred writer called earthly, sensual, devilish. There is an appearance of gentleness, but the voice betrayeth him. A.T. Robertson is the one open dissenter. He acknowledges that seeing pagan Rome in the first beast and papal Rome in the second has been the common Protestant interpretation since the Reformation, with undoubted verisimilitude in it, then says it is more than doubtful whether any such view comes within the horizon of the imagery; he prefers taking the first for imperial Rome and the second for the provincial power that imitated Rome in the persecutions, which would locate this beast in Asia Minor without world-wide scope. On the lamb-like horns he reports two commentators confessing themselves unable to make anything of the item, and offers the suggestion that the creature had the roar of a dragon with the looks of a lamb.

On the relation between them there is more agreement. Charles Ellicott puts it compactly: the second is not a successor but a supporter of the first, the intellectual force of an earthly wisdom made subservient to the spirit of unmitigated worldliness. Albert Barnes makes the two in reality one kingdom, the prolongation of the old Roman dominion, distinct enough in origin to need separate symbols, and observes that either would have fallen long since had the other not upheld it. Adam Clarke distributes the two horns to the secular clergy and the monastic orders, and reckons the mendicant friars the weightier of the two.
13:
On the wonders themselves they are unanimous that nothing is really done. John Gill calls them miracles not real but pretended, lying wonders of the kind the legends are full of. Albert Barnes is careful about the claim: the word is the one commonly used of miracles, and the representation is that this power founds its claim on pretended miracles and produces an effect on the world as if it wrought them; John describes him as he saw him, laying claim to the power. Why fire from heaven is specified he will not say for certain, only that such a sign would be among the most striking, as lying beyond all human power — the sign Elijah obtained on the sacrifice, and the one the disciples proposed against the Samaritans. A.T. Robertson gathers the same precedents and adds the warning: Christ promised great signs to the disciples, but warned them too against false prophets with their signs and wonders. Adam Clarke uses the wonders to fix the identification, since the same figure is later called the false prophet, and prophet in Scripture style is often a preacher or expounder of God’s word; the two-horned beast is therefore an empire of false teachers. Its wonders he lists as doctrines rather than portents — that the clergy are the only true ministers of Christ, that they can forgive sins and sell indulgences, and that prayers can deliver souls from a place he has fabled.

Who is deceived is answered three ways. John Gill restricts it absolutely: not the elect of God and true believers, who cannot be deceived by the signs of false Christs and false prophets, since the deceivableness of unrighteousness operates only in them that perish. Charles Ellicott makes the vulnerability moral rather than decreed: when men lose the will to ask whether a thing is right, they become easy prey to some specious deception, which is why a caution against immoral marvels is entered in both dispensations: mere greatness, of achievement or of miracle, is no guarantee of a good cause. He sets the two mottoes against each other, might is right for worldliness and right is might for faith, and says those who hold the second cannot worship the beast though the death-wound is healed. A.T. Robertson generalises furthest, noting that the verb is the one Christ used in saying the deception would reach the very elect if possible, and calling the public’s gullibility before new charlatans a constant cause for wonder.

What the image is divides them more. A.T. Robertson takes it concretely: the emperor’s image could be his head upon a coin, a figure woven on a standard, a bust, or a statue — anything people could be asked to bow down before, a test the provincial priests pressed as it was pressed at Rome. Adam Clarke insists on a person, and argues that it cannot be the emperor, who for all his title of supreme head of Christendom was only chief of the Germanic confederation; the image must be the supreme ruler of the whole Latin empire, and since the false prophet makes it, that ruler must be an ecclesiastic. Charles Ellicott keeps it moral: the beast deifies the spirit of worldliness, leading astray by subtlety rather than by real power. Albert Barnes spends his space instead on showing that the Papacy has in fact been kept up by delusion, quoting a historian’s remark that one great pontiff was always disposed to confirm religion by the evidence of ghosts and miracles, retailing from the Breviary a missionary who turned enough seawater fresh to save five hundred travellers and a friar who sailed a hundred and sixty miles on his cloak, and reporting that news has just reached his country of a city in Italy honoured because the eyes of a picture of the Virgin there had moved.
15:
The giving of breath to the image is where the historical readings part company most visibly. Albert Barnes begins from the powerlessness: the image has no life in itself, and the second beast imparts it, so that the image is invested with authority and exercises it. Taking the image for the Roman civil power restored, he looks for the fulfilment in some act of the Papacy by which an empire resembling the old one in jurisdiction received a vivifying impulse — power conferred from outside which it did not have in itself. The speaking he defines by what follows it, the issuing of an authoritative command that those who will not worship shall be killed.

Adam Clarke passes on a reading in which the image is a man. The influence of the corrupted clergy is seen, on this view, in inducing mankind to make an image to the wounded beast, and that image is the pope, properly the idol of the Church, representing in himself the whole power of the beast and the head of all authority, temporal as well as spiritual. He is nothing but a private person until the corrupted clergy by choosing him give life unto him and enable him to speak his decrees and persecute to death as many as refuse to submit. The ceremonial is the proof: once chosen he is clothed in the pontifical robes, crowned, placed upon the altar, and the cardinals kiss his feet in a rite called adoration — first they elect and then they worship, as an old medal has it, whom they create they adore. Clarke prefaces this with a parallel from another religion, that the Brahmins by incantation profess to give eyes and a soul to a newly made image, after which, being supposed the residence of the god it represents, it has a legal right to worship.

A.T. Robertson deflates the miracle without denying the history. The second beast, probably a system rather than a person, could work magical tricks of the kind conjurors have always worked; the word rendered life has here its original sense of breath, and the speaking image he takes for ventriloquism of the sort met with in the Acts. What he insists on is the penalty: he notes the threefold repetition of the image of the beast in one sentence, and cites a provincial governor’s letter to his emperor as evidence that refusing that worship carried capital punishment. Charles Ellicott declines the mechanism and reads the vitality as apparent: wisdom can give a semblance of life to the most doomed cause, since the bulk of mankind read only with their eyes and not at all with their thoughts.

On what the refusal costs, and what kind of homage is refused, they differ again. Albert Barnes is explicit that the worship here is civil and not religious homage, the image having power to set up its jurisdiction over men and secure their allegiance on pain of death. Charles Ellicott makes it religious and continuous: the emperor’s image was in ancient days an object of worship, and Christians suffered rather than prove disloyal to Christ by such an act, willing to render to Caesar the things that were Caesar’s but refusing to any but God the homage that belonged to God. He then generalises past both empire and papacy: the golden image is ever set up on the plains of this world, its glitter surviving the storm of the ages; it speaks and men adore, because they walk by sight and not by faith; and no imperial or papal edict is needed to doom to social death those who refuse to shape their conduct by self-interest, who are sure to be treated as fanatics because they follow right and conscience and Christ.
16:
The three pairs are read as a figure of universality. Albert Barnes works through them: small and great divides mankind by age, stature and rank; rich and poor divides the same whole another way; free and bond a third, since all the dwellers on earth are one or the other. None are exempt, neither the mighty who might be beyond control nor the humble who might be beneath notice; and the jurisdiction he has in view has been as absolute over kings as over the poor.

What the mark is divides them. Adam Clarke reaches his answer by cross-reference, since the same mark is later called the mark of his name: the name of the beast being the Latin empire, the mark of his name must be Latin worship. He points to the mass and the offices, which are in Latin and contain the sum and substance of that worship, and calls it the badge distinguishing the Latin Church from all others on the face of the earth, the only infallible mark by which a genuine papist can be known. He adds that the right hand, used figuratively in Scripture, stands for the physical power of the person spoken of. Albert Barnes keeps it general: something was branded on the man showing that he belonged to the beast, as a slave carried his master’s name. A.T. Robertson answers from documents: the word comes from a verb meaning to engrave, and the papyri show that official business documents often carried the name and image of the emperor with the date as an official stamp, this very word being the name of that seal. He notes that animals and slaves were branded with the owner’s name, as Paul bore the marks of Christ, that one ancient ruler compelled some Jews to receive the mark of a god as his devotees, and that another commentator derives the metaphor from the phylacteries worn on hand and forehead. On the right hand means in plain sight.

The prohibition on buying and selling they document from opposite ends of history. A.T. Robertson calls it plainly a regular boycott against all who were not worshippers of the emperor, and observes that the stamp might bear either the name or the number, the two being one and the same, since numbers were written with letters — a reckoning, one scholar suggests, intelligible to the writer and his Asian readers but not to others. John Gill takes the trade in both senses, ecclesiastical and civil: to hold church office, say mass, hear confession, give absolution or sell pardons, and also to trade and exercise merchandise; and he cites the decrees: a Lateran council forbidding any to trade with the Waldenses and Albigenses, a French synod forbidding communion with heretics in buying and selling, and a papal bull ordering that no contract be made with them. Adam Clarke quotes the same canons and draws the rule from them: dissent from the authorised forms brings condemnation as heresy, and with it interdiction from commerce and all the benefits of civil society, the intention being that, deprived of the comfort of humanity, men may be compelled to repent. He reports the pitch reached in the tenth and eleventh centuries, when nobody might come near the excommunicated, not even their own wives, children or servants, who forfeited all legal rights and were excluded from every office; and he describes the form of the sentence, lighted torches thrown on the ground with curses and trampled out to the ringing of the bells.

Albert Barnes draws the principle rather than the instances, that where a power determines who may buy and sell it has absolute control over the wealth of the world, traffic being one of the principal means by which property is acquired.
18:
What sort of wisdom is called for is contested. John Gill reads the concealment as deliberate: wrapping the matter up so obscurely shows great wisdom in God, as it requires much in men and exercises their intellectual powers to find it out. Albert Barnes agrees that the task is difficult but not hopeless: a direct statement might have exposed the writer to persecution, and it is no indignity to an inspired book, since riddles and dark sayings were common in the early world. The verb, he notes, means to reckon with pebbles, so the reader is told to compute. Charles Ellicott resists that conception of the task. Is the wisdom that solves this the mere cleverness which can guess an acrostic, he asks, or the true heavenly wisdom, which is moral rather than intellectual? The dignity of the Apocalypse is sacrificed when we search its meaning like children playing with conundrums rather than like men guided by its principles. A.T. Robertson calls it a puzzle for which all sorts of solutions are offered.

Where a name is sought, the two Latin candidates split the field. Albert Barnes argues that the word must be Greek, since John wrote in Greek for Greek readers and the numerals are Greek, and settles on the word for the Latin man, which yields the number exactly and was proposed by a second-century father on the ground that Latins then reigned. He prefers it to Roman because the Western kingdoms took the name Latin for everything — the Latin church, the Latin clergy, the Latin councils, the mass and Scriptures all in Latin. Against the objection of a Jesuit controversialist that the word is properly spelt without the diphthong, he answers from the Greek spelling of Latin names and the older Latin habit of writing the long vowel as a diphthong. He lists the rival solutions offered, several of which also reach the number, and remarks how many point to Rome.

Adam Clarke takes the objection Barnes dismissed and makes it decisive: every Greek writer who uses the word spells it without the diphthong, so if that word were meant, its own number would have been given. Since the beast is a kingdom, the Greek for the Latin kingdom must carry the number, and he counts it out exactly, adding that no other kingdom on earth contains it. He then argues, against the prevailing opinion and a long list of authorities, that the second beast is numbered and not the first: the name of the beast and the number of his name are distinct, since a later vision names the beast, his image and the number as three things; and since the number is a man’s, the numbered beast must be one elsewhere represented as a man, which the ten-horned beast never is and the false prophet is.

A.T. Robertson reports the modern solution without adopting it: the Hebrew letters for Nero Caesar give the number, while the Latin form, lacking its final letter, gives six hundred and sixteen and so accounts for the variant reading. He calls this ingenious and possibly correct, then asks who can really tell. Charles Ellicott, who notes the same variant and favours the larger number, declines both names for a symbolic reading. The number is the threefold six, and its point is that it never reaches seven: with all its vaunted strength the beast is weak, with all its perfection imperfect, lacking the one needful thing. He takes it for a state of marvellous earthly perfection, when culture, civilisation, art, science and reason have combined to produce an age so nearly perfect that men begin to say faith in God is an impertinence and the hope of a future life a libel on the happiness of the present. Then only a wisdom from above will detect the difference between a world with faith and a world without it.
